summary:
Paraguay has no legal gender recognition procedure in force. The judiciary has yet to issue final rulings in ten lawsuits filed by trans people seeking recognition of their legal names, among them cases brought by Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepúlveda that have been pending since 2016. Both plaintiffs have taken communications to the UN Human Rights Committee under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and are awaiting a decision. Trans people are not allowed to change their name and gender on official documents, so a trans visitor whose passport marker conflicts with their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

Amnesty International's 2025-26 report records two trans migrants who were denied identity documents, evidence that the documentary gap reaches administrative encounters rather than staying theoretical.

There is no general anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime statute is recorded in the sources. A November 2015 bill to ban discrimination on those grounds has not advanced since its introduction. Protections that do exist are narrow and sector-specific, addressing sexual orientation in dormitory placement, violence against women, stateless persons, personal data and the internal staffing rules of one public office. None supplies a general remedy to a trans visitor refused service, accommodation or police assistance.

Violence and discrimination against LGBT people remain frequent in Paraguay and are often ignored by the police. An Associated Press report of September 2025 found that discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of their hometowns and into migration and sex work, a pattern that shapes the settings a trans visitor may move through.

Official hostility is documented at national and municipal level alike. The government banned discussion of LGBT issues in public schools in October 2017, and the Minister of Education said he might consider burning books that raise awareness about transgender people. Asunción's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March, per Amnesty International. Horacio Cartes, a senior ruling-party figure, said in 2017 that he would "shoot himself in the testicles" if his son married another man, later apologising to those offended.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised in Paraguayan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has held in an advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage; Paraguay is an OAS party and is bound by the ruling, while domestic law has not been brought into line. A trans visitor's partner therefore has no standing under local law.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Paraguay since 1990. The sources record an age of consent of 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct.

Healthcare carries one trans-specific entitlement. Resolution 695, approved by the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare in October 2016, requires that health service officials record and treat transgender patients under their identified social name on medical records, medical histories and forms. Law 7018 on Mental Health, enacted 15 November 2022, states that a mental health diagnosis cannot be made on the exclusive basis of sexual choice or identity.
tangentialFactors:
Amnesty International recorded 37 registered feminicides in Paraguay in 2025, and reported an April bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family. Both point to a narrowing of the institutional machinery that handles gender-based violence, although the figures are not trans-specific.

The historical baseline is severe. During the Stroessner dictatorship of 1954 to 1989 LGBT people faced heavy persecution; in the 1959 Caso 108, police arrested and tortured 108 gay men in Asunción and published their names, and the government publicly encouraged hatred and violence against LGBT people. The sources treat the current pattern of police inattention as continuous with that period rather than a break from it.

Paraguay's marriage law sits alongside that of Bolivia and Peru, which likewise recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, leaving several jurisdictions in the same position relative to the inter-American advisory opinion.

Regional comparisons cut both ways. Costa Rica implemented the same advisory opinion quickly, with about 300 people celebrating it at the court in January 2018, while Paraguayan commentary at the time framed the change as a difficulty the country still had to overcome.
localsOnly:
Adoption is not expressly closed to same-sex couples or to single men and women. Law 1136/97 restricts adopters only on grounds of infectious disease, mental disorder or a child-abuse record, leaving a gap in the statute that residents have read as permitting same-sex adoption in practice, against a society that still closes doors.

The limited anti-discrimination provisions operate in separate compartments. Law 5162/2014 requires that collective dormitory placement for adolescents take account of age, sexual orientation and degree of psychic development. Decree 6973 issued under Law 577/2016 protects women from violence without discrimination based on sexual orientation. Law 6149/2018 bars discrimination against stateless persons on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Law 6534/2020 treats sexual orientation data as sensitive personal data. Article 28 of the Ministry of Public Defense's internal rules prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation against its own employees. The November 2015 bill that would have generalised these protections has not moved since introduction.

The October 2017 school policy constrains what residents can encounter in public education: discussion of LGBT issues is banned in public schools, and the education minister floated burning books that raise awareness about transgender people.

Resolution 695 of October 2016 governs everyday healthcare contact for trans residents, obliging health service officials to use the patient's social name across records, histories and forms. Law 7018 on Mental Health, of 15 November 2022, bars a mental health diagnosis resting exclusively on sexual choice or identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory gives an outcome, a hearing date or an expected timetable for the ten name-recognition lawsuits or for the communications before the UN Human Rights Committee; both are recorded as pending with no decision.

Hate-crime legislation is not addressed anywhere in the inventory. Whether Paraguay has a statute covering offences motivated by gender identity, or what penalties such a statute would carry, is not sourced here.

Whether Resolution 695 remains in force, and how consistently hospitals and clinics apply the social name requirement, is not documented in the sources available for this entry.

The age-of-consent difference of 16 for homosexual conduct and 14 for heterosexual conduct rests on a secondary reference work rather than on a quoted provision of the Penal Code; the current statutory text is not reproduced in the inventory.

Amnesty International's count of identity-document refusals covers two trans migrants and no wider figure for refusals issued to trans people is available. The Asunción city council's ban on the commemorative event is reported without a date for the council decision, and the defender's death is given only as March.

Nothing in the inventory records whether the inter-American advisory opinion has been invoked in Paraguayan litigation to challenge the marriage bar, or how courts have responded.
